The two models agreed closely on which hints help. Their predicted hint effects were strongly correlated across the 40 hints of Study 1 (r = 0.85), and for 32 of the 40 hints the two predictions did not differ reliably (Fig. 7c). Each model was also correlated with the human hint effects (r = 0.73 for the Bayesian model and 0.83 for Centaur). Despite their different constructions, both models therefore capture which hints help people and in which tasks, and this pattern is not what separates them.

On the eight hints where the predictions differed, each model was closer to people on four distinct conditions (Fig. 7d). Centaur's three largest advantages, of 7 to 17 percentage points, were all value hints identifying the best arm, which people acted strongly on and the Bayesian model underestimated. The Bayesian model's advantages were smaller, 3 to 8 percentage points, and came from hints describing the task's structure or dynamics. Of these eight differences, only the one for the linear contextual hint "If the third number under the button is 1, you will get the most points." was reliably different from zero on its own, so we read the split as a consistent pattern across hints rather than as eight separate findings.

The Bayesian model fits human choices slightly less well than Centaur. However, the Bayesian model, provided the generative structure of the eight task types and a hand-specified meaning function for each hint, gives a normative account of the integration of language and experience with only two fitted parameters (T and γ). Centaur, which receives only the text of the task, hint, and history and has one fitted parameter (β), proves to be highly predictive of human choice patterns yet does not explain how these information sources combine. The two models thus serve as complementary tools for understanding how language shapes human experience and learning.

3 Discussion

Language and direct experience both contribute to the decisions we make. In this paper, we explore if there are coherent principles that guide their integration. We created a novel setting, the Instructed Bandit Tasks, to systematically study how people use language while learning from experience. The hints we studied occupy a different niche than the informationally equivalent descriptions studied in the description-experience gap [12] literature. In our setting, verbal descriptions were partial, arrived amid ongoing experience, and more closely resembled the advice and tips that accompany everyday learning.

We found that hints differed in helpfulness under different task types, hints that were strictly true sometimes made learners reliably worse, and the same hint could help at one point and have no effect at another depending on how much experience the learner had accrued. These effects suggest that natural language does not contribute a fixed amount of information into the learning process, but instead reshapes a learner's hypothesis space of the current task world.

From this view, the function of language in learning is to reshape the learner's world model and reweight their task representations. We attempted to capture this by constructing a hierarchical Bayesian agent which encodes the semantics of each hint as a secondary prior weighting of its beliefs. The Bayesian framing then offers a normative account of the integration process, as both linguistic and experienced evidence are cast into the common currency of probability and combined via Bayes' rule. The fitted Bayesian model captured which hints help and in which tasks, and was highly interpretable, allowing us to trace in time as a learner's beliefs changed about the nature of the task. One limitation of this approach is the manual curation of the hints and meaning functions, which ablations show account for most of the model's fit (Appendix G and Fig. A2). One way to address this is to use LLMs to translate arbitrary natural language inputs into these formal constraints, in the spirit of the model synthesis architectures [16], which would also scale the approach beyond the set of hints studied here.

A central contribution of our paper is to compare this Bayesian account to that of a fine-tuned large language model. Fit only by rescaling its choice distributions, Centaur assigned the highest likelihood to the held-out human choices and reproduced the fine-grained behavioral signatures of the human data with highest fidelity, despite never having been trained on IBT (though Psych-101 includes other bandit tasks) or optimized for these metrics. Most notably, while the normative Bayesian agent captured cases where language reduces uncertainty in a verifiable way, Centaur reproduced human errors, such as when informative hints harmed performance and when the benefit of a hint faded with experience. That a model trained only to predict the next token of human choice sequences is able to predict the cases in which humans will act suboptimally supports that Centaur has implicitly learned the behavioral regularities of how language governs experiential learning in humans.

These approaches capture opposite sides of growing debates about approaches to cognitive modeling. Our results suggest that they might not be so incommensurate. There was significant alignment between Centaur and the Bayesian model in terms of prediction (r = 0.85 across hint effects; Section 2.4). The two models can also be used together in the spirit of scientific regret minimization [26], in which the cases where a predictive model like Centaur succeeds and a normative model fails identify revisions for the latter.

This work opens several new avenues for future research. Future work could test hints that are conflicting or wrong (as everyday advice often is) and which an account of language as world-model constraint predicts should mislead learners in equally systematic ways (cf. ref. [10]). As everyday advice often comes from speakers of varying knowledge and intent rather than a trusted experimenter, the IBT can be extended to probe how source credibility and other aspects of social cognition impact how learners integrate language [4]. More broadly, almost all tasks begin with instructions which participants hear or read and which set the frame for the current experiment, yet cognitive models almost universally do not model the instructions directly, PREPRINT instead assuming the model structure is in place already at the start of the task. This work starts to push at the boundaries of what we include in our psychological accounts of such tasks.

4 Methods

4.1 Behavioral experiment details

We conducted two behavioral studies with samples recruited on Prolific (https://prolific.com/). Study 1 evaluated participants across all task and hint pairings in the IBT, surveying the space of scenarios in which language can influence experiential learning. Study 2, designed to follow up on the findings of Study 1, manipulated the trial at which the hint appeared in order to test how accumulated experience changes the integration of linguistic information. Neither study was preregistered, and all analyses are exploratory.

We recruited 340 participants in Study 1 and 300 in Study 2. Participants self-reported their gender, which was not analyzed (Study 1: 176 men, 157 women, 3 preferred not to say, 1 other; Study 2: 140 men, 157 women, 2 preferred not to say, 1 other). Sample sizes were not determined by an a priori power analysis. A simulation-based sensitivity analysis (Section 4.6 and Appendix D) indicates that our design afforded 80% power to detect task-level hint effects of 2.1 to 10.6 percentage points of the arm spread depending on task. Minimum detectable effects for individual hints ranged from 2.2 to 13.3 percentage points, and for individual hint-by-onset conditions in Study 2 from 3.8 to 8.9.

We filtered out any participants who did not complete all games (2 people) or failed the instruction comprehension quiz more than twice (1 person), leaving N=337 and N=300 for analysis, respectively. We limited participation to adults from English-speaking countries (the US and UK) to ensure a baseline language competency. Participants were aged 18 to 80 (mean 42.7) in Study 1 and 19 to 79 (mean 40.9) in Study 2. We paid all participants at a rate of $15/hour with an additional bonus of up to $1.00, calculated proportionally to their performance in a randomly selected game trial (to avoid declining motivation later in the experiment). Participants completed the experiment in a median of 12.4 minutes in Study 1 and 9.1 minutes in Study 2. All procedures were approved by the NYU Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent before beginning the experiment.

In Study 1, participants played up to 15 games (see Appendix D for the composition of the Study 1 sample). Each game was assigned a random configuration of task type and hint, sampled from our pre-defined IBT dataset. In Study 2, each participant played 12 games. Each game was assigned one of two task types: stationary, in which experience alone rapidly identifies the best arm, and the patch foraging task, in which the non-stationary reward structure makes experiential learning substantially harder. This let us test the sensitivity of hint timing to task context while keeping the design tractable. Each game was also assigned a hint timing parameter, which determined the trial (of [0, 4, 8, 12]) on which the hint would appear on the screen. Both experiments used a within-subjects design, but because game conditions were assigned randomly, our analyses mix within-and between-participant comparisons. In each game, participants were instructed to maximize their point earnings over 20 or 40 trials, depending on game type (two context, three context, and Bernoulli games had double the number of trials due to task complexity). We kept the number of experiential trials relatively small in order to avoid overwhelming the information contributed by language.

The participants had to choose between 5 lettered buttons on the screen by clicking the buttons. Each time they made a choice, their action and observed reward were logged in a running history table under the buttons, to reduce the load on memory. In some games, a hint was provided at the top of the screen. In Study 1, the hint was always present to the participant, and in Study 2, the hint was made visible only after a predetermined number of choices, altering the amount of prior experiential learning the subject had before being given a hint. In the two context and three context cases, the participant also saw a shape (of circle, square, or triangle) on the screen at each trial to indicate which context they are in, and the context is additionally logged to the history table (Appendix H and Fig. A3). Both of our behavioral tasks were programmed using the Smile (https://smile.gureckislab.org/) project.

4.2 A Bayesian model of instructed learning

An IBT learner should best estimate the means of the Gaussian arms in order to make optimal selections and maximize their expected rewards. As rewards are noisy and observed only for the arm that was chosen, these estimates are inherently uncertain and built incrementally over trials. One way to model these beliefs is with a Bayesian RL framework, where the learner's knowledge is represented as a probability distribution over the arm means and is updated after every trial. Beyond providing a principled account of uncertainty, the Bayesian model allows for an additional language-informed prior to dually factor into the posterior belief.

At each timestep t, the learning agent chooses an action a t and observes a reward r t drawn from the taskspecific reward function. The observation history is given by the full sequence of actions taken and rewards received, h t = (a 1 , r 1 , a 2 , r 2 , . . . , a t , r t ), and is sometimes annotated by additional contexts or features. In the absence of language, RL is purely evaluative [2], and the only learning signal comes from these observed rewards. In this case, we can use Bayes' Rule to represent the agent's posterior distribution over the N arm means given h t as:

Under total uncertainty, the prior P 0 (µ 1:N ) is broad, and we use a Normal prior centered on the typical arm value (Appendix I). In order to explore effectively, the agent must sample actions via Thompson sampling and iteratively update its beliefs to optimize the likelihood of the observations [14, 27].

In both real world settings and in the IBT, however, the learner faces an additional challenge of determining which problem structure they are learning under before estimating the parameters of the problem. We thus introduce a hierarchical Bayesian model which maintains uncertainty over both task types and parameters. Letting τ ∈ {stationary, drifting, two context, three context, time delayed, patch foraging, Bernoulli, linear contextual} denote the task type and θ τ be the task specific parameters, the posterior of the hierarchical Bayesian model can be represented as:

The likelihood P (h t | τ, µ 1:N , θ τ ) encodes the generative model for each type. We use closed-form conjugate updates (Normal-Normal for most of the tasks) to compute this term. For types with unknown hyperparameters, the model uses Monte Carlo marginalization by sampling θ τ from the current type-specific priors and averaging over the resulting likelihoods. After each trial, the hierarchical Bayesian agent updates its joint beliefs over task types and parameters, P (τ, θ τ | h t ). Implementation details for each agent type are given in Appendix I. We additionally verify that the Bayesian hierarchical agent can correctly recover each of the task types in Appendix I and Fig. A4. To test which components of the agent account for its fit to human choices, we also fit ablated variants that drop the hint weight, replace the hierarchy over task types with a single stationary bandit, or fix the task type to its true value (Appendix G).

A key challenge is how to map the information from the natural language hints onto the learning problem. As a motivating example, consider a learner given the hint "The value of arm 1 is greater than 25". If the learner had first sampled arm 2 and observed a reward of 100, they would immediately recognize arm 2 to be a good choice, whereas if they had sampled arm 3 and received a reward of 0, they might be tempted to exploit arm 1 instead. The key point being, information contained in the hint, combined with individual experience, can rapidly shift choice behavior. Thus, we propose that the learning agent may use the information from the hint as a secondary Bayesian prior [21] [22] [23] to alter its beliefs over the task representations. In particular, this term, representing the natural language information, should remain distinct from the prior over tasks and over parameters (these reflect something about the learner's understanding of the games or the world at large), combine with the observations, and additionally inform the posterior beliefs.

with estimating the mean of each of the N Gaussian distributions corresponding to the arms. The parameter space that captures all possible arm mean configurations can then be defined as Θ = R N . A natural language hint, l, places constraints on this space by essentially ruling out particular combinations of parameters from the possible worlds. To capture the semantics (i.e., which possible worlds are retained or excluded given a hint), we construct a "semantic meaning function" f l , which is a mapping from the task parameterization to some real number indicating truth value [4, 28]. More concretely, we define f l : Θ → R ≤0 ∪ {-∞}.

The extended real-valued functions allow us to capture categorically true or false hints, represented by 0 or -∞ respectively, as well as graded similarity judgments between parameter values in a manner analogous to fuzzy logic used in control engineering [29]. A toy visualization of how the hints translate to meaning functions and to probabilistic weightings over possible worlds is shown in Fig. 2a. The meaning functions of the Bayesian model were fixed before Studies 1 and 2 were run.

While the first two examples in Fig. 2a visualize the weighting functions for value-based hints, other hints might weight the agent's belief over the task types (as in the third example), the sampled parameters, or the agent's action and reward history. For example, a hint advising the agent to continue trying other arms throughout the game will use the trial time since the last selection of an arm as a weighting to upsample environments in which the best arm is one that the agent has not chosen recently. In this way, all types of hints in the IBT dataset change the agent's likelihoods for selecting possible environments, thereby constraining the agent to only worlds consistent with the hint. We can then adapt equation ( 2) by adding the meaning function weights as a secondary prior:

In equation ( 3), exp(γf l (τ, µ 1:N )) introduces the language dependency on the agent's posterior. The exponential maps the hint output (in (-∞, 0]) into the probabilistic space for compatibility, and γ adds flexibility to the model by allowing variation in the weight of language on the learning process. Because hints that rule out possible worlds outright assign them a value of -∞, and hence a weight of 0 (and a value of 0, or a weight of 1, to those consistent with the hint), γ only changes the influence of soft hints, such as those that weight samples by the agent's choice history. Algorithmically, the agent first computes the experienceonly posterior, samples a large batch of K hypothetical environments from this standard posterior and passes them through the meaning function to evaluate their compatibility with the linguistic hint. Finally, the agent resamples a single environment from this weighted batch via importance sampling [30], selects the optimal action in that specific sampled environment with Thompson sampling [14], and executes the action to observe the next reward. Over the learning process, the agent maintains hierarchical beliefs to jointly infer task type and parameters. The language-informed hierarchical Bayesian RL agent is able to model the optimal learner through all of the problems in the IBT. In each scenario, the agent is provided no hint or one of the hints corresponding to the task type.

4.3 Centaur on IBT

To assess whether state-of-the-art large language models harness the information from linguistic hints in sequential decision-making tasks, we evaluate variants of the Centaur model on IBT. Centaur is a large language model fine-tuned on Psych-101, a large-scale dataset of past psychological experiments translated into text-based prompts [25]. Psych-101 includes a number of multi-armed bandit experiments, so Centaur has been trained on human choices in related paradigms, but the IBT tasks and hints are not part of it. The fine-tuning objective was to align the base model, Llama 3.1 70B [24], to human behavior by matching token likelihoods to human choices. One claim is that Centaur can predict human behavior for new behavioral tasks given only the relevant task instructions. We were interested in evaluating it on IBT to carefully measure the impact that different hints would have on prediction behavior for a model that relies heavily on linguistic input. We linearized our instructions and tasks following the protocol in [25], making only minimal changes to the text provided in the behavioral experiment to fit the query structure in the Psych-101 training dataset.

To simulate each of the games, we iteratively passed as input the task instructions, trial relevant contexts, and history of past choices and rewards to the models. We then extracted the predicted logits over the five valid action tokens (integers 1-5) and normalized via softmax (with generation temperature of 0.8 [25]) to obtain a probability distribution over the arm choices. We ran the models on each task 100 times while randomly rotating the arm mean configuration to avoid numerical biases, then averaged the per-trial choice distributions across simulation runs to yield mean model probabilities for each task type, hint, and trial condition.

4.4 Fitting models to human choice

We fit each model to the choices of 337 participants using 5-fold cross-validation and a maximum-likelihood approach to compare how well each model accounts for human decision-making. For the hierarchical Bayesian agent, we find the softmax temperature T and the weight of the linguistic hint γ which maximize the likelihood assigned to the true human choices at each trial. First, we iteratively pass each action and reward from the human trials to the hierarchical Bayesian agent, simulate the belief update, then draw 500 weighted posterior samples over task type and parameters. We then count the Thompson sampling actions across arms to construct a distribution over all actions. For the language-informed hierarchical Bayesian agents, we additionally reweighted the posterior samples by the hint function raised to the power of γ to simulate the effect of the hint. The reweighted action counts then pass through a softmax function with temperature T to produce the model's choice probabilities for that trial. We precomputed these statistics for every trial, so that fitting T and γ required only closed-form likelihood evaluations over the cache. We optimized both parameters using L-BFGS-B via the multivariate optimizer function scipy.optimize.minimize [31], with bounds T ∈ [0.1, 20.0], γ ∈ [0.1, 20.0]. In every fold, γ sat at its lower bound. Refitting with the lower bound widened to 0.001 left T unchanged to two decimals and changed the held-out log-likelihood by at most 0.0002 nats per trial, so the bound does not affect the reported fits.

For Centaur, we introduced a rescaling parameter T that rescales the LLM's predicted choice distribution by a factor of β = T ref /T : P (a) = p(a) β a ′ p(a ′ ) β β > 1 sharpens and β < 1 flattens the rescaled probability distribution over action tokens. We fit β by extracting the choice probabilities at each trial of each game and scaling the distribution by this factor using the bounded scalar optimization function in Scipy (scipy.optimize.minimize scalar with bounds β ∈ [0.1, 20.0]). We additionally fine-tuned Centaur on a training subset of the human bandit choices (Cen-taurIBT) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) by training with a cross-entropy loss over the five arm tokens. Additional implementation details on fine-tuning as well as an analysis of how additional training sharpened the choice distributions are in Appendix F. Finally, we include a LLaMA baseline, the untuned Llama 3.1 70B model on which Centaur is built, scored on the same trials as Centaur, to isolate the contribution of Centaur's training on the Psych-101 dataset. The latter two models were fit with the same temperature procedure as Centaur. We evaluate all models on the held-out fold with the mean log-likelihood per trial, or the probability the model assigns to the human's actual choice (results in Section 2.4).

4.4.1 Model simulations

After the fitting procedure, we set the best-fit hint weight for the hierarchical Bayesian agent and temperature for Centaur and forward simulated each model to reproduce the behavioral dataset. For the Bayesian model, we ran 100 independent agent simulations per MAB type and hint condition on freshly sampled bandit environments. For Centaur, we prompted the model with the same text prompts used in the human task and sampled choices at each trial under the fitted temperature, yielding 100 simulated games per MAB type and hint condition. We then analyze the hint effects of each of these datasets as compared to the behavioral dataset with the procedure in Section 4.5.2.

4.5 Statistical analyses

We use two complementary analyses matched to two questions. Paired t-tests on early versus late trial regret verify that each task is learnable from experience alone, and linear mixed models, with participant random intercepts, estimate the task-level hint effects, the effect of each individual hint, and, in Study 2, how each effect changes with hint onset, while accounting for repeated measures and unequal games per condition.

4.5.1 Human learning t-tests

To verify that participants learned within each task type from experience alone, we used only no-hint games and compared mean regret in the first five trials to mean regret in the last five trials using paired t-tests. For each task type, we computed the average regret (the difference between the mean of the optimal arm and that of the chosen arm, expressed as a percentage of the game's arm spread) of the participants over these two windows. A positive difference between mean regret in early and late trials indicates improvement over the course of the game. t : mean difference SE of difference is the difference relative to the variability. We report two-sided p-values, adjusted with the Holm-Bonferroni procedure [32] across the eight tasks. All eight human tests remain significant after correction. Full results are in Appendix C.

4.5.2 Linear mixed model fitting

We used a linear mixed model to quantify the effect of each hint on task performance for both humans and model simulations. For people, we fit the model (neg regret ∼ hint + (1|subject)) separately for each task type to predict the negative mean per-trial regret, expressed as a percentage of the game's arm spread (higher is better) with hint condition as a fixed effect and with a participant random intercept to correct for individual variation. Task-level hint effects were estimated with the same model, treating all hinted games as a single condition. For the models, which lack individual variation, we fit the model (neg regret ∼ hint) by ordinary least squares with heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors. For Study 2, the model was fit separately for each task type and hint onset, with both hinted and no-hint games restricted to post-onset trials and, at onsets 4, 8, and 12, the game's mean regret before the onset included as a covariate (there are no pre-onset trials at onset 0). Each mixed model was estimated by restricted maximum likelihood using the statsmodels library [33]. We report estimated differences, 95% confidence intervals, and two-sided p-values for each task type and hint combination. The p-values are adjusted for multiple comparisons with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure [34], applied separately to the 8 task-level effects, the 40 hint effects of Study 1, and the 40 hint-by-onset effects of Study 2. Adjusted p-values and significance stars are reported for the human effects only. To test whether hint effects in Study 2 depended on onset, we compared each hint's effect at trial 0 with its effect at each later onset (trials 4, 8, and 12) using a Wald test on the difference between the two estimates, and adjusted the 30 contrasts with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. We draw upon this modeling framework throughout our behavioral analyses.

4.6 Sensitivity analysis

We conducted a simulation-based sensitivity analysis [35] to estimate the minimum detectable effect (MDE) [36, 37] of our experiment design at each level of inference reported in the paper: per-task aggregate hint effects (Fig. 3b), per-hint effects within task (Fig. 4), and per-timing effects in Study 2 (Fig. 5). For each, we fit a reduced linear mixed model (neg regret ∼ hint + (1 | subject)) to the corresponding data to estimate the between-participant standard deviation τ and residual standard deviation σ. Holding fixed the number of participants, number of games per participant, and hint assignments for each condition, we then simulated synthetic datasets under a grid of true hint effects δ, refit the model to each, and tested for an effect using our reported convention (two-sided test at α = .05, before the correction for multiple comparisons applied in Figs. 4 5.

D.3 Detection criterion

The main analyses report hint effects from linear mixed models, starring effects whose adjusted two-sided p-value is below .05. Across the 88 × 13 × 1,000 model fits, our sensitivity simulations use the same mixed model with a two-sided Wald test at α = .05 (|z| > 1.96) as the detection criterion, without the correction for multiple comparisons applied in the main analyses. The two-sided test addresses both beneficial effects and harmful hint effects like those reported in Figs. 4 5.

D.4 Results

Per-cell results for Study 1 are reported in Table A4, and the Study 2 cells are available in the code repository (Code availability, main text). First, the two task types played by the largest share of participants (stationary and patch foraging) had the sharpest task-level resolution (MDEs of 2.1 and 2.3 percentage points of the arm spread), while the six task types assigned to participant subsets required larger effects (5.9 to 10.6 percentage points), with time delayed among the highest owing to its substantially larger residual variability (σ = 23.8). Second, per-hint cells required correspondingly larger effects (MDEs of 2.2 to 13.3 percentage points across tasks), due to the smaller sample sizes per hint. Third, Study 2's per-hint-by-onset cells had MDEs of 3.8 to 8.9 percentage points, and all five significant Study 2 effects exceeded their MDE.

Two of the four task-level effects reported as reliable in the main text exceeded their task's MDE, while two fell just below it (7.1 observed against an MDE of 7.4 for two context, and 10.4 against 10.6 for linear contextual), and we accordingly treat their magnitudes as approximate. The MDEs also indicate that only large hint benefits were reliably detectable in the drifting, three context, and Bernoulli tasks, so the lack of aggregate hint effects (see Results in the main text) should not rule out the possibility of moderate effects. At the per-hint level, 12 of the 13 significant effects (starred conditions in Fig. 4) exceeded their specific MDE. The remaining one was still detected despite an observed magnitude below its 80%-power threshold, as true effects below the MDE may still be detected with lower probability. This implies that this estimate of a hint effect is more susceptible to magnitude overestimation, as when power is low, the detected experiments are more likely to have noise inflation. We interpret this effect, the harmful structure hint in the Bernoulli task (observed 9.9 vs. MDE 10.8), whose direction is supported (p = .024), as evidence of effect direction rather than precise effect size.

Task-level MDEs ranged from 2.1 percentage points of the arm spread (stationary) to 10.6 (linear contextual), with the two tasks played by the largest share of participants (stationary and patch foraging) resulting in the sharpest resolutions (MDEs of 2.1 and 2.3) owing to their larger samples. The remaining one was detected despite falling below it, and we treat its magnitude as approximate (Appendix D).

Appendix Appendix A IBT task definitions

To ensure our findings generalize beyond any single problem structure, we constructed the Instructed Bandit Tasks (IBT) to span a wide array of bandit variants commonly studied in the reinforcement learning and cognitive science literature. The eight task types were chosen to systematically vary the computational demands placed on the learner. Each task type admits a different family of linguistic hints about its underlying structure, making the set well suited for studying how instructions interact with qualitatively different learning problems. Appendix C Learning in each task

This section reports the full learning-verification statistics summarized in the Methods of the main text. Table A3 gives the per-task paired t-tests for human participants and both model simulations, computed on no-hint games only. Fig. 3 in the main text shows the corresponding learning curves and hint effects. The Bayesian agent learned in all eight task types (t range 8.22-21.50, all p < .001). Appendix D Sensitivity analysis

We did not preregister our experiments or determine sample sizes via an a priori power analysis. Thus, we conducted a simulation-based sensitivity analysis [35] to understand the minimum detectable effect (MDE), or the smallest true hint effect that the design would detect with 80% probability [37], of each condition in our experimental design. This provides a condition-specific benchmark against which detected effects can be interpreted [36].

D.1 Composition of the Study 1 sample

The Study 1 sample combines two batches. In the first, 159 participants each played 15 games, each assigned a random configuration of task type and hint sampled from the pre-defined IBT dataset. The second comprises 178 participants who completed the first build of the Study 2 experiment, in which every hint appeared at trial 0; we included their games with hints from the Study 1 hint set (10 per participant, all stationary or patch foraging). Because Study 2 drew its trial-0 conditions from the same sessions, 74 of these participants also contribute games to Study 2, and 740 games appear in both datasets.

D.2 Procedure

We computed MDEs at three levels, namely (a) task-level aggregate hint effects (Fig. 3b; 8 cells), (b) per-hint effects within task (Fig. 4; 40 cells), and (c) per-hint effects at each onset in Study 2 (Fig. 5; 40 cells). For each, we fit a linear mixed model (neg regret ∼ hint + (1 | participant)) to the subset of the data to derive the between-participant standard deviation τ and residual standard deviation σ.

We then simulated synthetic datasets with the same participants, number of games per participant, and hint assignments as the original games and generated outcomes with y ij = δ • hint ij + u i + e ij , where u i ∼ N (0, τ² ) is a participant-level offset, e ij ∼ N (0, σ2 ) is game-level noise, and δ is a planted true hint effect. We analyzed each synthetic dataset with the same mixed model and recorded whether the hint effect was detected (criterion below). For each condition, we swept δ over a 13-point grid spanning 0 to 1.25 times

Appendix E Fine-grained choice trajectory metrics

To assess fine-grained behavioral alignment between models and human participants, we computed three metrics from the sequence of arm choices a 1 , a 2 , . . . , a T over a game of T trials.

Switch Rate Switch rate measures the proportion of trials on which the agent changed its choice relative to the previous trial: where 1[•] is the indicator function.

Higher values indicate more exploratory behavior.

Choice Entropy Choice entropy measures the uniformity of arm selection over the full game using the Shannon entropy of the empirical choice distribution: where K is the number of arms and pk = 1 T T t=1 1[a t = k] is the empirical frequency of arm k across trials.

Higher entropy indicates more uniform exploration across arms.

Exploitation Onset Exploitation onset measures how early an agent committed to a single arm, defined as the normalized trial index of the first occurrence of five consecutive identical arm choices: We fine-tuned Llama-3.1-Centaur-70B [25] on human bandit choices using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [49], implemented via Unsloth with 4-bit quantization. The model was loaded in 4-bit and adapted with LoRA applied to all attention and MLP projection matrices, with rank r = 16, α = 16, and dropout = 0.05.

Fine-tuning followed the same participant-level 5-fold cross-validation as the other models (Methods, main text): in each fold, the model was fine-tuned on the training participants (about 269) and evaluated on the held-out participants (about 68), so that no participant's choices appeared in both. At each trial, the full game history up to that point was formatted into the same prompt used during simulation, and the model was trained to predict the human's next arm choice. Rather than standard cross-entropy over the full vocabulary, we used a choice-restricted loss, where logits were extracted only for the five arm-choice tokens, and label smoothing (ϵ = 0.05) was applied to prevent overconfidence.

We fine-tuned Centaur for 2 epochs with AdamW (lr = 2 × 10 -5 , weight decay = 0.01), batch size 4 with gradient accumulation over 2 steps (effective batch size 8), gradient clipping at 1.0, and a cosine learning rate schedule with a 5% linear warm-up. Maximum sequence length was 1,024 tokens. Hyperparameter choices were largely set to default. Fine-tuning was run on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU with 128 GB of host memory and was allocated a 12-hour wall-time limit on an HPC cluster node.

Fig. A1 shows the rank-ordered average choice probability for the base Centaur model and the fine-tuned CentaurIBT model. We observe that fine-tuning on IBT sharpens the distribution. CentaurIBT concentrates 88.6% of probability mass on the top-ranked arm on average, as compared to the 79.0% for base Centaur. This overconfidence is the primary reason that CentaurIBT under-performs across IBT tasks in Fig. 7a.

When the model's top-ranked arm does not match the human choice, the log-likelihood is severely penalized as the probability mass is low on all other arms. This indicates that either higher label smoothing or entropy regularization may be required during fine-tuning in order to improve model prediction. We asked which components of the Bayesian model account for its fit to human choices and for its predicted hint effects. To do so, we fit ablated variants of the model with the same five-fold cross-validation and fitting procedure as the full model (Methods, main text), changing only the ablated component.

G.1 Ablated variants

• No hint. Drops the hint weight from equation (3) entirely, including for hard hints, and fits only the softmax temperature. The agent learns from experience alone.

• Non-hierarchical. Replaces the hypothesis space of eight task types with a single stationary bandit. Value and history hints still act on the sampled arm means, but hints about the task type or about parameters a stationary bandit lacks (e.g., the delay or the linear-contextual features) have no effect.

• Fixed type. Gives the agent the true task type, so it infers only the parameters within that type. Hints that act only on the task type have no effect.

• Shuffled hint. A control for the content of each hint. Each hinted game is scored with the meaning function of a different hint from the same task, one the participant did not see but that is still true of the game. We cycled through each task's hint list, giving four shuffled variants.

G.2 Fitting and comparison

Held-out negative log-likelihood is averaged over the eight tasks with equal weight, because stationary and patch foraging have about twice as many participants as the other tasks. (Averaged over trials instead, as in the main text, the full model's value is 1.300 nats per trial.) Differences between variants are tested with paired t-tests over participants. Because the task-weighted means and the per-participant differences weight the data differently, the gap between two task-weighted means need not equal the mean per-participant difference.

In every hinted variant, the hint weight γ sat at its lower bound of 0.1 in all five folds. This is expected: γ scales only the soft, history-based hints (Methods, main text), and the fit prefers them as weak as allowed.

Widening the bound to 0.001 gave γ = 0.001 in every fold, left T unchanged to two decimals, and changed the held-out negative log-likelihood by at most 0.0002 nats per trial. The bound is therefore immaterial.

G.3 Results

First, we find that language accounts for most of the fit (Fig. A2). Removing the hint weight raised the heldout negative log-likelihood from 1.315 to 1.403 nats per trial (per-participant difference 0.11 [0.10, 0.12], p < .001). The hint-blind model also predicted no hint effects: its correlation with the human per-hint effects was r = 0.09, against 0.73 for the full model.

Next, we verified that hint benefits depend on their task content. Scoring games with a different, still-true hint from the same task fit almost as poorly as no hint (1.383-1.391 nats), and the predicted hint effects no longer tracked those of people (r between -0.25 and 0.25).

Removing the hierarchy cost very little overall (1.346 nats; per-participant difference 0.007 [-0.001, 0.015], p = .086), but this near-zero difference hides two opposing effects. The hierarchy fit choices better in tasks whose structure a stationary learner cannot represent (three context, time delayed, and linear contextual) and worse in tasks that people treated as simple bandits (Bernoulli, drifting, and patch foraging), where uncertainty over task type made the agent explore more than people did. Without the hierarchy, model correlation with human effects also dropped from 0.87 to 0.05 for policy hints and from 0.43 to 0.12 for structure hints, while the correlation for value hints did not drop (0.49 and 0.67).

Finally, the skyline Bayesian model is task-specific. In this case, giving the agent the true task type indeed improved fit (1.306 nats; per-participant difference 0.011 [0.008, 0.014], p < .001) and the correlation with human hint effects (r = 0.79), at the cost that hints acting only on the task type have no effect.

Appendix I Implementation details of hierarchical Bayesian agents

The hierarchical model maintains a posterior P (τ, θ τ | h t ) over eight task types. Each type implements a conjugate or Monte Carlo likelihood. All types use a shared Normal-Normal arm mean prior with µ0 = 45, σ0 = 20, which approximates the mean and spread of the given arm values.

I.1 Computing type specific likelihoods

Stationary The agent runs a closed-form Normal-Normal update. At each trial t, the predictive variance for arm a is σ 2 a + σ 2 obs,a , where σ 2 a is the current posterior variance of arm a's mean, and σ 2 obs,a is the known observation noise, which is set to the bandit arm's standard deviation. After observing reward r, the posterior precision is updated as λ ′ a = λ a + 1/σ 2 obs,a and the mean as µ ′ a = (µ a λ a + r/σ 2 obs,a )/λ ′ a . Drifting For drifting bandits, the agent uses a Kalman filtering framework [40] to track non-stationary means by marginalizing over a distribution of drift rates ϵ ∼ N (µ ϵ , σ 2 ϵ ) (prior µ ϵ = 2, σ ϵ = 1) and growing the posterior variance by the sampled ϵ 2 at each timestep to enforce a recency bias on observations. The log marginal likelihood is estimated via Monte Carlo over 10 sampled ϵ values. The posterior belief over ϵ is updated via importance-weighted moment matching on the samples.

Time delayed

The agent maintains a categorical distribution over delay values k ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} with uniform prior. For each candidate k, it computes the Normal-Normal log marginal likelihood by pairing each observed reward at trial t with the action taken at trial t -k. The posterior P (k | h t ) is updated via Bayes' rule.

Patch foraging

The agent models a deterministic transition where arm means deplete when chosen and replenish otherwise by marginalizing over a change rate λ ∼ N (µ λ , σ 2 λ ) with prior µ λ = 0.2, σ λ = 0.08, using 40 Monte Carlo samples. After observing a chosen arm a, its mean is multiplied by e -λ and all other arms are multiplied by e +λ , capped at a running estimate of each arm's equilibrium mean, updated online from observations. The posterior over λ is again updated via importance-weighted moment matching.

Two context and three context The agent maintains independent Normal-Normal arm mean posteriors for each context (2 or 3, respectively). Only the beliefs associated with the current context index (provided as side information from the trial history) are updated at each trial. The log marginal likelihood sums over context-appropriate observations only.

Bernoulli For Bernoulli bandits, the agent performs a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate update to estimate the success probabilities of each arm, with prior Beta(α 0 , β 0 ) = Beta(1, 1) per arm. Rewards are in {0, 100}, and any other observed reward sets the log likelihood to -∞, falsifying the Bernoulli hypothesis. Wins increment α a , and losses increment β a.

Linear contextual

Finally, for the linear contextual bandits, the posterior is a multivariate normal over the weights of the linear model. The agent performs standard Bayesian linear regression [50] to maintain a covariance matrix for the 3-dimensional features, with a Gaussian prior θ ∼ N (0, 100I). After each trial, the posterior is updated in closed form from the observed feature and reward pairs. The expected reward for an arm is then the dot product of its features with the sampled weights.

I.2 Updating posteriors and selecting actions

After computing log likelihoods ℓ τ = log P (h t | τ ) for each type, the type posterior is updated as: with uniform prior P (τ ) = 1/8 at t = 0, using log-sum-exp normalization for numerical stability.

I.3 Action selection with and without hints

The agent uses Thompson sampling to select actions. At each trial, K = 500 samples (τ (i) , µ (i) 1:N , θ (i) τ ) are drawn from the current posterior P (τ, µ 1:N , θ τ | h t ). When a hint l is present, each sample is reweighted by: where f l is the hint meaning function defined in the Methods of the main text and γ is the fitted hint strength parameter.

A single hypothesis is then resampled from this weighted population (or uniformly if no hint) via importance sampling [30], and the agent's action is the greedy arm, a (i) = arg max a µ (i) a , of that resampled hypothesis. The resulting reward is observed and the trial data (a, r) is appended to the history h t before the next belief update.

I.4 Type recovery

We conducted a type recovery analysis using the actual parameters from the behavioral experiment (five arms with means [10, 20, 40, 60, 80] and σ = 5) to assess whether the hierarchical Bayesian agent can correctly identify which of the eight task types it is observing. For each task, we simulated 20 independent games using a random policy. After observing the full sequence of actions and rewards for each game, we performed a single batch belief update and recorded the agent's posterior P (type | data) across the eight candidate types. We averaged the agent's posteriors across the 20 repetitions per type.

Fig. A4 shows the resulting confusion matrix. Each row corresponds to the true task type used to generate the data, and each column corresponds to the agent's posterior belief of a given type. Four task types, Bernoulli, two context, three context, and linear contextual, are identified with near-perfect accuracy. Time delayed yielded strong posteriors (0.92). The agent was moderately confused between stationary and drifting as expected. With only 20 trials and a drift rate of ε = 2, the reward variance attributable to drift is small relative to observation noise, making the two distributions nearly indistinguishable. Finally, patch foraging is the most difficult to identify (0.46 correct), with residual mass split between stationary (0.25) and drifting (0.27). This is justified by the fact that depletion and replenishment signals are extremely difficult to detect under random exploration, as they require arms to be chosen repeatedly. Overall, the analysis confirms that the agent is well-calibrated for the structurally distinctive task types and that confusions are confined to the tasks that are genuinely hard to distinguish from random-policy observations.
